In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Surah al-Qiyamah (The Resurrection)

The discussion on the interpretation of His saying:

[5] ﴿Nay, but man desires to continue in wickedness before him.﴾

﴿Nay, but man desires to continue in wickedness before him.﴾ That is, to persist in wickedness throughout the time that lies ahead of him, nothing turning him from it, and never repenting of it.

Al-Shihab said:

أمامَهُ (amamahu, "before him") is an adverb of place (ẓarf makan), used here metaphorically for the future time, so it conveys continuity. The pronoun refers to man, or to the Day of Resurrection. It has also been said that it conveys perpetuity and continuance, because the verse informs about the state of the wicked person: that he desires to commit wickedness in the future. His desire and his assumption are themselves the very essence of wickedness. Repeating the noun (the explicit term "man" rather than a pronoun) carries an evident threat and a condemnation of the ugliness of what he has committed, and it indicates that humanity itself rejects it. It has also been said that he understood it as continuance so that the transition (al-idrab, a shift from one subject to another) would be valid, and the meaning becomes: "Nay, but man desires to continue in his wickedness and not repent. For this reason he denied the resurrection (al-ba'th)."

Al-Qashani said: That is, to persist in wickedness by inclining toward bodily pleasures and animal appetites, plunging his head into them, throughout the time that lies before him, both present and future. So he is heedless of the Resurrection because his sight does not reach it, because he is confined to fleeting pleasures, because of his excessive greed for them, and because he is veiled by them from the everlasting life. He asks about it, mocking and deeming it unlikely, as He, glorified is He, said:

**On the interpretation of His saying, the Exalted:**

[6–13] ﴿He asks: When is the Day of Resurrection?﴾ ﴿So when the sight is dazzled﴾ ﴿and the moon is eclipsed﴾ ﴿and the sun and moon are joined together﴾ ﴿on that Day man will say: Where is the escape?﴾ ﴿No! There is no refuge!﴾ ﴿To your Lord on that Day is the place of rest﴾ ﴿On that Day man will be informed of what he sent forward and put off.﴾

﴿He asks: When is the Day of Resurrection?﴾ That is: when will it occur? (He asks) in disbelief and mockery. The clause is a resumption (istinaf), or a circumstantial clause (hal), or an explanation of His saying "yafjur" (he wishes to persist in sinning), or a substitute for it. The resumption is explanatory (bayani), as if it were said: Why does he want to persist in immorality? It was answered: Because he denied the resurrection and mocked it.

﴿So when the sight is dazzled﴾ That is: it becomes bewildered and astonished, at what has come from the command of Allah. Mujahid said: That is, at the time of death.

﴿And the moon is eclipsed﴾ That is: its light goes away.

﴿And the sun and moon are joined together﴾ That is: they are brought together in the going away of light, so that neither of them has any light. It was said: They join together and then they are folded up, as His saying, Exalted is His praise: ﴿When the sun is folded up﴾ [al-Takwir: 1]. Ibn Zayd said: They are brought together, and then they are cast down onto the earth.

﴿On that day man will say: Where is the escape?﴾ That is: the flight. That is: he seeks a place of escape and refuge because of his bewilderment, or he says the words of one in despair, knowing that there is no escape at that time.

﴿No!﴾ is a rebuke to him for seeking an escape. ﴿There is no refuge!﴾ That is: there is no shelter.

﴿To your Lord on that Day is the place of rest﴾ That is: the resting place of the servants, whether Fire or Garden. That is: their resting place is entrusted to Him alone and not to anyone else, or the settling of their affair, and the judgment concerning them.

﴿On that Day man will be informed of what he sent forward and put off﴾ That is: of his deeds that necessitate his salvation and reward, of good works and righteous deeds, ﴿and put off﴾ That is: from it, so he neglected and fell short in it and did not do it.

Al-Shihab said:

"What he sent forward" is a metaphor for what he did, and "what he put off" is what he left and did not do. This is a well-known figurative usage in what has been mentioned. Or: "what he sent forward" is what he himself did, and "what he put off" is the deeds of those who followed his example after him, which are counted as if they were done by him.

Al-Qaffal permitted that "then" (*thumma*) may be for sequence in reporting; that is, "We inform you that upon Us is its explanation," and therefore it does not indicate the permissibility of delaying the explanation beyond the time of address. Al-Razi criticized this, saying that it is abandoning the apparent meaning without evidence.

[20–25] ﴿Nay, but you love the hasty life﴾ ﴿and neglect the Hereafter﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 21] ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22] ﴿looking toward their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 23] ﴿And faces that Day will be scowling﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 24] ﴿expecting that a backbreaking calamity will be inflicted upon them﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 25]

﴿So he neither believed﴾, i.e., in the religion and the Book. Or: "he did not give in charity his wealth," i.e., he did not pay its zakat. ﴿Nor prayed﴾, i.e., the prayer, which is the head of the acts of worship, which he neglected.

﴿But he denied﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 32], i.e., instead of affirming. ﴿And turned away﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 32], i.e., instead of the prayer through which complete devotion to Allah, Exalted is He, is achieved. ﴿Then﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 33], i.e., along with these shortcomings toward Allah, Exalted is He, ﴿he went to his family, swaggering﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 33], i.e., he strutted in his walk. Its root is yatamattat, meaning he stretches himself out, because the one who struts stretches his steps.

Remarks:

The first: The pronoun in the verses refers to the man mentioned earlier in His words, ﴿Does man think﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 36].

The second: al-Razi said: He, Exalted is He, explained how this man behaved in matters related to the foundations of the religion and its branches, and in matters related to his worldly life. As for what relates to the foundations of the religion, he did not affirm the religion but denied it. As for what relates to the branches of the religion, he did not pray but turned away and withdrew. As for what relates to his worldly life, he went to his family strutting and swaggering in his walk.

The third: The verse indicates that the disbeliever deserves blame and punishment for abandoning the prayer, just as he deserves them for abandoning faith.

The fourth: al-Razi said: The people of Arabic grammar said: "lā" here is in the position of "lam," so His words ﴿So he neither believed nor prayed﴾ mean: he did not believe and he did not pray. It is like His words ﴿But he did not attempt the steep ascent﴾ [al-Balad: 11], i.e., he did not attempt it.

Likewise is what is narrated: "Have you seen one who neither ate, nor drank, nor cried out (at birth)?" Al-Kisa'i said: I have not seen the Arabs utter a single word in such a context alone, until they follow it with another, either explicitly or implicitly. As for the explicit, they do not say, "Neither Abdullah is going out," until they say, "nor so-and-so," and they do not say, "I passed by a man who does not do well," until they say, "nor does he act well." As for the implicit, it is like His words ﴿But he did not attempt the steep ascent﴾ [al-Balad: 11], then the speech is interrupted and He says ﴿And what will make you know what the steep ascent is?﴾ [al-Balad: 12] ﴿It is the freeing of a slave﴾ [al-Balad: 13] ﴿or feeding on a day of severe hunger﴾ [al-Balad: 14]. The implied meaning was: "neither freed a slave nor fed a needy person," and he sufficed with it once. Some of them said: the implied meaning in His words ﴿But he did not attempt﴾ [al-Balad: 11] is: "Then why did he not attempt?" and "Why did he not attempt?" End of quotation.

﴿Woe to you, and woe!﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 34] ﴿Again, woe to you, and woe!﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 35], i.e., woe to you, time after time. It is an invocation against him that what he dislikes befall him, in repeated and multiplied succession.

It has also been said: the meaning is: "Distance for you, then distance in your worldly affairs, and distance for you, then distance in your affairs of the Hereafter." Al-Razi related this from al-Qadi, then said: al-Qaffal said: this admits of several meanings.

The first: that it is a threat initiated by Allah against the disbeliever.

The second: that it is something the Prophet ﷺ said to his enemy, meaning Abu Jahl, and that enemy of Allah disdained it out of his pride in himself, so Allah sent down something similar to it.

The third: that it is a command from Allah to His Prophet to say it to the enemy of Allah. The meaning would then be: "Then he went to his family, swaggering; so say to him, O Muhammad: Woe to you, and woe!, i.e., beware, for what you cannot withstand of harm has drawn near to you." End of quotation. The first is the most apparent.

A subtle point:

Interpreting ﴿Woe to you﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 34] as "woe to you" (waylun laka): al-Shihab said: it expresses the meaning intended by it, for it is like it, so it is used for invoking against him, or for threat and warning.

And from al-Asma'i: it is used to express regret over a matter that has passed.

This is the intended meaning of it. As for the discussion of its wording, it has been said: it is a past-tense verb of supplication from the patron (waliyy), and the lam is extra; i.e., may Allah bring upon you what you dislike. Or the lam is not extra, i.e., may destruction draw near to you. Close to this is al-Asma'i's statement that its meaning is: that which would destroy him has come near to him to befall him. Tha'lab approved of this.

It has been said: it is a noun whose pattern is af'al, from the word waylun, and it was transposed. It has been said: it is fa'la, and therefore it is not given tanwin. Its meaning is what has been mentioned, and its alif is for lengthening rather than for feminine marking. On the nominal reading it is a subject (mubtada'), and "laka" is the predicate. It has been said: it is an invariable verb-noun (ism fi'l mabni), and its meaning is: "May evil follow you after evil."

Al-Zamakhshari reported from Abu Ali that it is a proper name for the meaning of waylun, and it is not declined because of its being a proper noun and its fi'l pattern. It has been objected to this: waylun is not inflected, and like "yawmun aywam" it is not analogical, and it is not used apart from the qualified noun. Claiming transposition without evidence is not accepted, and a generic proper name lies outside analogy, so what has been mentioned is far-fetched in several respects. It has also been said: the best view is that it is an elative (af'al al-tafdil) predicate of an implied subject, supplied as fits its context. So the estimate here is: (p-6001) "The Fire is more fitting for you," meaning: you are more deserving of it and worthy of it. End of quotation.

﴿Does man think that he will be left neglected?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 36], i.e., left without command, prohibition, or recompense, even though man is the one endowed with reason, taught eloquence, and created with the disposition to live in society, and given among the gifts what has distinguished him over others. Part of completing the kindness toward him is rescuing him from his bewilderment, informing him of the path of guidance, and not leaving him stumbling in the wilderness of his ignorance. This was by the grace and favor of Allah, as He indicated by His words: ﴿Was he not a drop of semen emitted?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 37], i.e., poured into the womb. ﴿Then he became a clinging clot﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 38], i.e., blood. ﴿And He created﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 38], i.e., He determined his limbs. ﴿And proportioned﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 38], i.e., He made those limbs proper for their functions and balanced. ﴿And made of him two mates﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 39], i.e., two kinds, ﴿the male and the female﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 39], i.e., for the preservation of his species, populating the world until the term He decreed and determined.

﴿Is not He able to give life to the dead?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 40], i.e., so that He brings them into being after their death for the building of the Hereafter.

It has been narrated that the Prophet ﷺ, when he recited it, would say: "Glory be to You, and yes indeed (fa-bala)." Abu Dawud related it from a man among the Companions. He also related it from Abu Hurayrah with the wording: whoever recites ﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 1] and reaches ﴿Is not He able to give life to the dead?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 40], let him say: "Yes (bala)." Imam Ahmad and al-Tirmidhi also related it. And Allah knows best.
